summary.text: Chemistry is the science of matter, studying what it is made of, how it is built, and how its properties and behavior change in reactions.
It focuses on atoms, where rearranging the bonds that hold them together can turn some substances into different substances.
It is sometimes called the central science because it underlies fields such as botany, geology, pharmacology, and forensics.

facts.label: Atomic number
facts.value: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus

facts.label: Carbon isotopes
facts.value: Carbon atoms have 6 protons and mass number 12 or 13

facts.value: An atom's radius is about 10,000 times its nucleus's

items.prompt: A chemist balances the equation for a transformation and finds the atom counts on the two sides are unequal. What does that signal?

options.label: The change formed a mixture rather than a compound
The change took place without any glass equipment
The change is a nuclear reaction or radioactive decay
The change turned a solid into a plasma

items.explain: In a chemical transformation the number of atoms on the left and right of the equation is equal. When it is unequal, the change is called a nuclear reaction or radioactive decay.

items.prompt: A student expects a compound to look and behave like a blend of the elements it contains. What does chemistry say?

options.label: Its properties bear little similarity to those of its elements
Its properties are an average of those of its elements
Its properties match those of its most plentiful element
Its properties match its elements only when it is pure

items.explain: A compound is a pure substance made of more than one element, and its properties bear little similarity to those of its elements.

items.prompt: Two atoms each have 6 protons in the nucleus, but one has a mass number of 12 and the other 13. What are they?

options.label: Atoms of two different elements
Two compounds made from the same elements
One neutral atom and one charged atom
Two isotopes of the same element

items.explain: The number of protons sets the element, here carbon. Atoms of one element with different mass numbers are isotopes.

items.prompt: An atom is full of charged particles, yet a plain atom is electrically neutral overall. Why?

options.label: The uncharged neutrons carry a charge that cancels the protons
The negative electrons balance out the positive protons
The nucleus holds no charge, and the electrons carry none either
The protons and electrons both carry a negative charge

items.explain: Protons are positive and electrons are negative, so in a neutral atom the electrons balance out the protons. Neutrons are uncharged.

items.prompt: The standard chart of the chemical elements lines them up in a fixed order. What decides that order?

options.label: How heavy each element's mass number is, lightest first
The year in which each element was discovered
The number of protons in each atom's nucleus
How easily each element joins in a reaction

items.explain: The periodic table orders elements by atomic number, the number of protons in the nucleus.

items.prompt: A friend says that if there is no lab equipment made of glass, it cannot be real chemistry. Is that right?

options.label: No, much experimental and industrial chemistry is done without it
Yes, since glass equipment is what defines the field
Yes, though only in industrial settings
No, because chemistry happens only on paper

items.explain: Glassware is the stereotype of a chemistry lab, but it is not central to chemistry, and a great deal of experimental and industrial chemistry is done without it.

pack.title: The central science
pack.question: What do chemists study, and why does it reach into so many other fields?

beats.title: The central science
beats.hook: A few kinds of atoms, rearranged, make everything from rocks to medicines.

beats.prompt: You heat a sample and a new substance forms. At the smallest scale, what changed?
beats.explain: A chemical reaction transforms substances into different substances by rearranging electrons in the bonds between atoms, so the atom count stays equal on both sides.

choices.label: The atoms grew in size until they became new ones
choices.feedback: The atoms stay the same; only how they are joined changes.

choices.label: Each atom gained or lost protons in its nucleus
choices.feedback: Changing protons would change the element, which is not what a chemical reaction does.

choices.label: The electrons in the bonds between atoms were rearranged
The atoms vanished and different atoms appeared
choices.feedback: It looks like things disappeared, but the atom counts match on both sides of the equation.

beats.prompt: Match each term to what it means.

right.label: Pure substance of more than one element
Number of protons in the nucleus

beats.explain: Protons set the element, neutrons change the mass number, and a compound combines more than one element.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which one?

steps.text: All atoms with 6 protons in their nuclei are carbon.
One sample has atoms with mass number 12, and another has atoms with mass number 13.
Different mass numbers mean the two samples are different elements.
So the second sample cannot be carbon.

beats.explain: An element is set by its number of protons. Atoms with the same atomic number but different mass numbers are isotopes of one element.

beats.prompt: Sort each part of the atom by where it sits.
beats.explain: The nucleus is made of protons and neutrons, together called nucleons, while the electrons make up the cloud around it.

beats.idea: Chemistry studies how atoms and their bonds rearrange, which is why it underlies so many other sciences.

paragraphs.heading: What chemistry studies
paragraphs.text: Chemistry is the science of matter: what it is like and how it behaves. It is a physical science that looks at what matter is made of, how it is put together, its properties, and how all of these change when substances react with one another. It also asks what the chemical bonds inside compounds are like. In its range of subject matter, it sits between physics and biology.

paragraphs.heading: The central science
paragraphs.text: Chemistry is sometimes called the central science, because it gives a base for understanding many other fields, both pure and applied. It helps explain how plants grow, how igneous rocks form, how ozone forms in the atmosphere and how pollutants break down. It also reaches into how medicines act, what the soil on the Moon is like, and how DNA evidence is collected at a crime scene.

paragraphs.heading: From alchemy to chemistry
paragraphs.text: People have practised chemistry under different names since ancient times. The word itself is a Renaissance reworking of alchemy, an older set of practices that mixed chemistry with metallurgy, philosophy, astrology, astronomy, mysticism and medicine. Alchemy is often linked with the hunt to turn lead and other base metals into gold, yet alchemists also cared about many questions that modern chemistry asks. The word alchemy comes from the Arabic al-kīmīā, which may trace back through Greek to Kemet, the old Egyptian name for Egypt.

paragraphs.heading: Atoms at the core
paragraphs.text: The atom is chemistry's basic unit. It has a dense core, the atomic nucleus, made of positively charged protons and uncharged neutrons, with a cloud of negatively charged electrons around it. In a neutral atom the electrons' negative charge balances the protons' positive charge. The core is tiny but heavy: a proton or neutron has about 1,836 times the mass of an electron, while the whole atom is about 10,000 times wider than its nucleus.

paragraphs.heading: Elements and isotopes
paragraphs.text: A chemical element is a pure substance made of just one kind of atom. What fixes the kind is the number of protons in the nucleus, called the atomic number and written Z. The mass number counts protons and neutrons together, and atoms of one element can differ in it; such variants are called isotopes. Every atom with 6 protons is carbon, for example, but carbon atoms can have mass numbers of 12 or 13. The periodic table lays out the elements by atomic number, in columns called groups and rows called periods.

paragraphs.heading: Reactions and compounds
paragraphs.text: A chemical reaction turns some substances into one or more different ones. Underneath, the electrons in the bonds between atoms are being rearranged. A chemical equation writes this down, and the count of atoms on its left side matches the count on its right; if the counts differ, the change is a nuclear reaction or radioactive decay instead. A compound is a pure substance made from more than one element, and its properties bear little resemblance to those of the elements in it.
